claim: Myosin V and VI are antagonistic motors that cohabit membrane vesicles in cells.
source: Myosin V and VI are antagonistic motors that cohabit membrane vesicles in cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: DNA nanostructures with myosin V and VI display solely unidirectional movement on both single actin filaments and keratocyte actin networks.
source: While scaffolds display solely unidirectional movement, their directional flux is modulated by both actin architecture and the structural properties of the myosin lever arm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2 and 3, demonstrating unidirectional trajectories.

claim: The directional flux of scaffolds is modulated by actin architecture.
source: While scaffolds display solely unidirectional movement, their directional flux is modulated by both actin architecture and the structural properties of the myosin lever arm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing 1D actin filaments vs 2D keratocyte networks shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The directional flux of scaffolds is modulated by the structural properties of the myosin lever arm.
source: While scaffolds display solely unidirectional movement, their directional flux is modulated by both actin architecture and the structural properties of the myosin lever arm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with chimeric myosins shown in Figure 6.

claim: Directional flux can be finely-tuned by the relative number of myosin V and VI motors on each scaffold.
source: This directional flux can be finely-tuned by the relative number of myosin V and VI motors on each scaffold.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing linear relationship between motor number and directional flux.

claim: The ratio of motor stall forces is a key determinant of the observed competitive outcomes.
source: Pairing computation with experimental observations suggests that the ratio of motor stall forces is a key determinant of the observed competitive outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling presented in Figure 5 paired with experimental observations.

claim: Traditional reconstituted systems to study membrane traffic do not incorporate the effects of actin-myosin interactions.
source: However, traditional reconstituted systems to study membrane traffic do not incorporate the effects of actin-myosin interactions (Lee et al., 2004; Zanetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Unconventional myosins are necessary for timely membrane traffic.
source: Additionally, while unconventional myosins are necessary for timely membrane traffic, their functional role is not apparent in live cell studies (Hasson et al., 1997; Sahlender et al., 2005; Hartman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional role of unconventional myosins is not apparent in live cell studies.
source: Additionally, while unconventional myosins are necessary for timely membrane traffic, their functional role is not apparent in live cell studies (Hasson et al., 1997; Sahlender et al., 2005; Hartman et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin V and VI co-reside on membrane vesicles in neuronal growth cones.
source: In this study, we focus on myosin V and VI, two opposing unconventional myosins that co-reside on membrane vesicles in neuronal growth cones (Suter et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Suter et al., 2000.

claim: Myosin V has been implicated in secretory traffic.
source: Myosin V has been implicated in secretory traffic, whereas myosin VI facilitates timely endocytosis (Suter et al., 2000; Kneussel and Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI facilitates timely endocytosis.
source: Myosin V has been implicated in secretory traffic, whereas myosin VI facilitates timely endocytosis (Suter et al., 2000; Kneussel and Wagner, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin V and VI are considered evenly matched antagonistic motors.
source: In the case of myosin V and VI, they are considered evenly matched antagonistic motors (Trybus, 2008; Spudich and Sivaramakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myosin V binds membrane cargo as dimers through a coiled-coil motif following its lever arm that natively homodimerizes it.
source: Both motors are thought to bind membrane cargo as dimers; myosin V through a coiled-coil motif following its lever arm that natively homodimerizes it, and myosin VI presumably through dimeric adaptor proteins that link it to cargo (Mehta et al., 1999; Buss and Kendrick-Jones, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI presumably binds membrane cargo through dimeric adaptor proteins that link it to cargo.
source: Both motors are thought to bind membrane cargo as dimers; myosin V through a coiled-coil motif following its lever arm that natively homodimerizes it, and myosin VI presumably through dimeric adaptor proteins that link it to cargo (Mehta et al., 1999; Buss and Kendrick-Jones, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and includes speculative language ('presumably').

claim: Myosin V homodimers have a step size of 36 nm.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI homodimers have a step size of 30 nm.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin V homodimers have stepping kinetics of 12 s−1.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI homodimers have stepping kinetics of 9 s−1.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin V homodimers have a stall force of approximately 3 pN.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI homodimers have a stall force of approximately 2 pN.
source: Homodimers of either myosin move processively on actin filaments with similar step sizes (V—36 nm; VI—30 nm), stepping kinetics (V –12 s−1; VI –9 s−1), and stall forces (V ∼3 pN; VI ∼2 pN) albeit in opposing directions (Mehta et al., 1999; Rief et al., 2000; Rock et al., 2001; Nishikawa et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2003; Altman et al., 2004; Uemura et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All myosin levers, with the exception of myosin VI, swing towards the barbed (plus) end of the actin filament.
source: All myosin levers, with the exception of myosin VI, swing towards the barbed (plus) end of the actin filament.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about myosin mechanics.

claim: A unique insert in myosin VI reverses the direction of its lever stroke towards the pointed (minus) end of the actin filament.
source: In the case of myosin VI, a unique insert reverses the direction of its lever stroke towards the pointed (minus) end of the actin filament (Liao et al., 2009; Spudich and Sivaramakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The myosin V lever consists of six light chain binding IQ-motifs wrapped with calmodulin light chains.
source: The myosin V lever consists of six light chain binding IQ-motifs wrapped with calmodulin light chains (Trybus, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The myosin VI lever is composed of two calmodulin-binding IQ-motifs followed by a pliable proximal tail domain, and a semi-rigid single α-helical domain.
source: The myosin VI lever is composed of two calmodulin-binding IQ-motifs followed by a pliable proximal tail domain, and a semi-rigid single α-helical domain (Spudich and Sivaramakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ali et al. (2011) reported that tethering a single myosin V and a single VI homodimer on a quantum dot leads to unidirectional motion on single actin filaments, with myosin V dominating the competition (79% of processive runs towards the plus-end of actin filaments).
source: Ali et al. (2011) reported that tethering a single myosin V and a single VI homodimer on a quantum dot leads to unidirectional motion on single actin filaments, with myosin V dominating the competition (79% of processive runs towards the plus-end of actin filaments).
evidence: This claim reports findings from a previous study by Ali et al.

claim: DNA nanostructures containing two myosin V and two myosin VI molecules interacting with a keratocyte-derived actin network show solely unidirectional movement.
source: We recently extended this finding to DNA nanostructures containing two myosin V and two myosin VI molecules interacting with a keratocyte-derived actin network (Hariadi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: On keratocyte-derived actin networks, myosin V and VI were evenly matched (52% of processive runs towards the keratocyte cell periphery).
source: While we did observe solely unidirectional movement, in contrast to Ali et al. (2011), myosin V and VI were evenly matched in our system (52% of processive runs towards the keratocyte cell periphery).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Scaffolds with both myosin V and myosin VI (1V:1VI) commit to a single direction on actin filaments (>99%).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Ali et al., 2011; Hariadi et al., 2014), scaffolds with both myosin V and myosin VI (1V:1VI) commit to a single direction on actin filaments (>99%; Figure 2B) with no directional reversal detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The movement of 1V:1VI scaffolds on single actin filaments is dominated by plus-end directed movement (Φout = 68 ± 1%).
source: The movement of 1V:1VI scaffolds on single actin filaments is dominated by plus-end directed movement (Φout = 68 ± 1%; Figure 2E), which is qualitatively consistent with previous observations using quantum dot scaffolds (79% plus-end directed [Ali et al., 2011]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and compared to previous literature.

claim: For 1V:1VI scaffolds moving along 2D keratocyte actin networks, both plus and minus-end directed movement is equally represented (Φout = 52 ± 1%).
source: In contrast to single actin filaments, both plus and minus-end directed movement is equally represented (Φout = 52 ± 1%; Figure 2E) for 1V:1VI scaffolds moving along 2D keratocyte actin networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The discrepancy between previous reports using quantum dots and DNA nanostructures stems primarily from the actin architecture.
source: Hence, the discrepancy between previous reports using quantum dots (Ali et al., 2011) and DNA nanostructures (Hariadi et al., 2014) stems primarily from the actin architecture.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing experimental results on different actin architectures.

claim: The origami scaffold commits to a single direction, either towards the cell periphery or the cell center, in every combination of myosin V and VI tested.
source: In every combination, the origami scaffold commits to a single direction, either towards the cell periphery or the cell center (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relative number of scaffolds that move to the cell center and cell periphery varies linearly with the fraction of myosin V or myosin VI.
source: The relative number of scaffolds that move to the cell center and cell periphery (Φout or Φin), however, varies linearly with the fraction of myosin V or myosin VI (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: The speed of nanostructures (1V:1VI) along actin filaments is significantly slower than nanostructures containing only two myosin V (2V:ØVI) or two myosin VI (ØV:2VI).
source: The speed of nanostructures (1V:1VI = (+) 162 ± 7 nm/s; (−) 66 ± 5 nm/s) along actin filaments is significantly slower than nanostructures containing only two myosin V (2V:ØVI = (+) 273 ± 8 nm/s) or two myosin VI (ØV:2VI = (−) 130 ± 7 nm/s) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The speed of nanostructure movement on the keratocyte network decreases as the difference in the number of the two motor types approaches zero.
source: Likewise, the speed of nanostructure movement on the keratocyte network decreases as the difference in the number of the two motor types approaches zero (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All of the motors can continuously interact with the actin tracks and collectively engage in competition.
source: Based on the reduction in speed for antagonistic ensembles, as compared to groups of one myosin type, we hypothesized that all of the motors can continuously interact with the actin tracks and collectively engage in competition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observed speed reductions, later tested with photo-cleavage experiments.

claim: Removal of one myosin type from the competition increases the speed and results in a single direction of movement.
source: Regardless of which motor type is cleaved, removal of one myosin type from the competition increases the speed and results in a single direction of movement (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by photo-cleavage experimental data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: All motors, regardless of type, are able to access the actin tracks and engage in continuous competition.
source: The directional switch and increase in speed after photo-cleavage indicate that all motors, regardless of type, are able to access the actin tracks and engage in continuous competition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the photo-cleavage experimental results.

claim: The collective movement is due to a continuous interaction of both motor types, and not due to detachment of losing motors from the actin track (or scaffold), when overpowered by the winning motor.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the collective movement is due to a continuous interaction of both motor types, and not due to detachment of losing motors from the actin track (or scaffold), when overpowered by the winning motor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations including speed reduction and photo-cleavage experiments.

claim: Myosin V changes the trajectory shape of ensembles of myosin V and VI on 2D actin tracks.
source: Lastly, the underlying continuous interaction is also consistent with our previous observation that myosin V changes the trajectory shape of ensembles of myosin V and VI on 2D actin tracks (Hariadi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: A motor can only perform a forward step if the resulting inter-motor tension (T) is less than its stall force.
source: Our model assumes that a motor can only perform a forward step if the resulting inter-motor tension (T) is less than its stall force (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an assumption in the computational model.

claim: For equally matched motors (rs = 1), there is an equal probability of trajectories moving in either direction (Φout = 50%).
source: For equally matched motors (rs = 1), there is an equal probability of trajectories moving in either direction (Φout = 50%).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: For ∆T/Flow < 0.5, the inter-motor tension exceeds the stall force of the weaker motor, with the stronger motor winning most of the competitions (Φout > 80%).
source: For ∆T/Flow < 0.5, the inter-motor tension exceeds the stall force of the weaker motor, with the stronger motor winning most of the competitions (Φout > 80%).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: For 0.5 < ∆T/Flow < 1 and stochastic stepping, there is a finite and increasing probability of inter-motor tension exceeding the stall force of the stronger motor, resulting in the weaker motor winning the competition (60% < Φout < 80%).
source: However, for 0.5 < ∆T/Flow < 1 and stochastic stepping, there is a finite and increasing probability of inter-motor tension exceeding the stall force of the stronger motor ('Materials and methods'), resulting in the weaker motor winning the competition (60% < Φout < 80%).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: The higher the kF/ks of a motor, the greater the ∆T when it steps forward on a 2D network.
source: On a 2D network, the higher the kF/ks of a motor, the greater the ∆T when it steps forward.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations on 2D networks.

claim: Linking a rigid motor (kF/ks >> 1; ∆Thigh) to a more flexible one (kF/ks << 1; ∆Tlow) is sufficient to systematically bias the competition in favor of the flexible motor.
source: For such simulations on 2D networks, linking a rigid motor (kF/ks >> 1; ∆Thigh) to a more flexible one (kF/ks << 1; ∆Tlow) is sufficient to systematically bias the competition in favor of the flexible motor (↓Φout with ↑∆Thigh/∆Tlow; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The greater flexural rigidity of myosin V compared to myosin VI is sufficient to equalize the competition on 2D networks.
source: Therefore, our simulations reveal that the greater flexural rigidity of myosin V compared to myosin VI is sufficient to equalize the competition on 2D networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational simulations paired with experimental observations.

claim: The outward flux for ensembles involving either chimera (1V/VI:1VI or 1VI/V:1V) on 2D actin networks are significantly higher than scaffolds with 1V:1VI.
source: The outward flux for ensembles involving either chimera (Figure 6A; i or ii) on 2D actin networks are significantly higher than scaffolds with 1V:1VI (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Balancing the tension per step (∆T) between the antagonistic motors is sufficient to restore the dominance of the stronger motor (myosin V) on 2D actin networks.
source: The higher outward flux indicates that balancing the tension per step (∆T) between the antagonistic motors is sufficient the restore the dominance of the stronger motor (myosin V) on 2D actin networks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chimera experimental results.

claim: Antagonistic motor ensembles display solely unidirectional movement.
source: We report that while antagonistic motor ensembles display solely unidirectional movement, as previously reported (Ali et al., 2011; Hariadi et al., 2014), their directional sorting can be linearly tuned by the relative number of the two motor types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Directional sorting of antagonistic motor ensembles can be linearly tuned by the relative number of the two motor types.
source: We report that while antagonistic motor ensembles display solely unidirectional movement, as previously reported (Ali et al., 2011; Hariadi et al., 2014), their directional sorting can be linearly tuned by the relative number of the two motor types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Directional sorting can be modulated independently by the myosin lever arm and the actin architecture.
source: Further, this directional sorting can be modulated independently by the myosin lever arm and the actin architecture.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different actin architectures and chimeric myosins.

claim: Competitive outcome is dependent on the ratio of the stall forces of the antagonistic motor types.
source: These observations support a simple generalizable model, wherein competitive outcome is dependent on the ratio of the stall forces of the antagonistic motor types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling and experimental observations.

claim: Scaffold run length linearly increases with motor number.
source: First, as previously reported (Hariadi et al., 2014), scaffold run length linearly increases with motor number (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that multiple motors on the same scaffold are capable of interacting with the actin network.
evidence: This claim refers to previous work and supplementary data.

claim: Multiple motors on the same scaffold are capable of interacting with the actin network.
source: First, as previously reported (Hariadi et al., 2014), scaffold run length linearly increases with motor number (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that multiple motors on the same scaffold are capable of interacting with the actin network.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that run length increases with motor number.

claim: The reduction in speed with both myosin subtypes is consistent with the trailing myosin interacting with the actin network.
source: The reduction in speed with both myosin subtypes is consistent with the trailing myosin interacting with the actin network, despite the unidirectional movement of the scaffold.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from speed measurements.

claim: The coordinated back-stepping of the trailing motor was observed by Ali et al. (2007).
source: This interpretation is consistent with the coordinated back-stepping of the trailing motor observed by Ali et al. (2007).
evidence: This claim refers to observations from a previous study.

claim: For scaffolds with both subtypes the speed decreases as the numbers of myosin V and VI are more evenly matched.
source: Third, for scaffolds with both subtypes the speed decreases as the numbers of myosin V and VI are more evenly matched.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The systematic reduction in speed argues for progressive engagement of additional antagonistic motors with the actin network.
source: This systematic reduction in speed alone argues for progressive engagement of additional antagonistic motors with the actin network.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the speed data.

claim: Removal of the antagonistic myosin leads to either an increase in speed (release trailing motor) or a reversal in direction (release leading motor).
source: Fourth, experiments with photo-cleavable myosin-scaffold linkages further show that removal of the antagonistic myosin leads to either an increase in speed (release trailing motor) or a reversal in direction (release leading motor) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by photo-cleavage experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ratio of the stall forces (rs = Fhigh/Flow) of the antagonistic motors is the key parameter that determines the outcome of scaffold sorting on 1D or 2D actin filament tracks.
source: Our model identifies the ratio of the stall forces (rs = Fhigh/Flow) of the antagonistic motors as the key parameter that determines the outcome of scaffold sorting on 1D or 2D actin filament tracks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational model.

claim: For ensembles with mismatched motors (rs > 2), the model predicts unidirectional movement led solely by the stronger motor.
source: For ensembles with mismatched motors (rs > 2), the model predicts unidirectional movement led solely by the stronger motor.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: For motors of similar strength (1 < rs < 2), the model predicts that either motor may lead the unidirectional motion, with the directional flux of scaffolds dependent on rs.
source: However, for motors of similar strength (1 < rs < 2), the model predicts that either motor may lead the unidirectional motion, with the directional flux of scaffolds dependent on rs.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: The model is in agreement with a recent report of unidirectional trajectories for DNA scaffolds linked to both kinesins and dyneins on 1D microtubules.
source: Further, the model is in agreement with a recent report of unidirectional trajectories for DNA scaffolds linked to both kinesins and dyneins on 1D microtubules (Derr et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim compares the model predictions to previous studies.

claim: The model differs from the bi-directional movement of isolated endosomes that are driven by a combination of native kinesin and dynein motors.
source: However, it differs from the bi-directional movement of isolated endosomes that are driven by a combination of native kinesin and dynein motors (Soppina et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim compares the model to observations from a previous study.

claim: Bi-directional movement of endosomes stems from the influence of additional regulatory elements on native endosomes.
source: We speculate, though, that bi-directional movement stems from the influence of additional regulatory elements on native endosomes (Kunwar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation with a citation.

claim: Motors with greater intra-motor torsional strain (rigid lever) experience a larger inter-motor tension per step and hence lose their competitive edge on 2D networks.
source: In essence, motors with greater intra-motor torsional strain (rigid lever) experience a larger inter-motor tension per step and hence lose their competitive edge on 2D networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling and experimental observations.

claim: The structural properties of the myosin lever arm control the directional flux of scaffolds on model cellular actin networks.
source: We find that the structural properties of the myosin lever arm control the directional flux of scaffolds on our model cellular actin network, thus having implications on sorting of vesicular cargo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with chimeric myosins.

claim: An extension of the myosin X lever arm is necessary for its preferential processive movement on parallel actin bundles, but not on single actin filaments.
source: For instance, an extension of the myosin X lever arm is necessary for its preferential processive movement on parallel actin bundles, but not on single actin filaments (Brawley and Rock, 2009; Nagy and Rock, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myosin VI has a unique three-helix bundle in its lever arm, which can unfold to alter the motor's structural properties.
source: Myosin VI, on the other hand, has a unique three-helix bundle in its lever arm, which can unfold to alter the motor's structural properties (Mukherjea et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: For groups of myosin V and VI, the flexibility of the lever arm controls trajectory shapes on 2D actin networks.
source: Furthermore, for groups of myosin V and VI, the flexibility of the lever arm controls trajectory shapes on 2D actin networks (Hariadi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: Single myosin V and VI have different stepping dynamics at actin filament intersections than on actin bundles.
source: For example, single myosin V and VI have different stepping dynamics at actin filament intersections (Ali et al., 2007) then on actin bundles (Ali et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual myosin V, VI, and X dimers show preferential motility on different actin architectures.
source: An in situ motility assay using detergent-extracted cells also reported that individual myosin V, VI, and X dimers show preferential motility on different actin architectures (Brawley and Rock, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The mesh size of the keratocyte actin network (∼30 nm) is comparable to the step size of myosin V (∼35 nm) and VI (∼30 nm).
source: Mesh size of the keratocyte actin network (∼30 nm) (Svitkina et al., 1995) is comparable to the step size of myosin V (∼35 nm) and VI (∼30 nm) (Rock et al., 2001; Yildiz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The keratocyte actin network is depicted by actin filaments oriented at ±35°, which corresponds to the characteristic Arp2/3 branch angle.
source: The keratocyte actin network is depicted by actin filaments oriented at ±35°, which corresponds to the characteristic Arp2/3 branch angle (Maly and Borisy, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The DNA nanostructure scaffold has six attachment sites at the vertices of a hexagon (35-nm side), yielding 122 unique myosin V and VI combinations.
source: Illustration of a programmable DNA scaffold (Rothemund, 2006) with six attachment sites at the vertices of a hexagon (dashed-line, 35-nm side), yielding 122 unique myosin V and VI combinations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with citation to the DNA origami method.

claim: Detergent-extracted keratocytes have a sufficiently large surface area (∼10 μm × ∼30 μm) allowing for simultaneous tracking of multiple myosin-labeled scaffolds.
source: For the 2D actin networks, we used detergent-extracted keratocytes (Hariadi et al., 2014) (Figure 1C), which have a sufficiently large surface area (∼10 μm × ∼30 μm) allowing for simultaneous tracking of multiple myosin-labeled scaffolds.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system with citation.

claim: The main core of the nanostructure is a flat rectangular DNA origami scaffold with 10.44 bp/turn, consisting of 24 DNA helices.
source: The main core of the nanostructure is a flat rectangular DNA origami scaffold with 10.44 bp/turn, consisting of 24 DNA helices (Woo and Rothermund, 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with citation.

claim: The scaffold is decorated with 23 Cy3 fluorophores to facilitate a high signal-to-noise ratio imaging.
source: The scaffold is decorated with 23 Cy3 fluorophores (shown as red light bulbs) to facilitate a high signal-to-noise ratio imaging.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myosin V and VI were engineered with SNAP tags for covalent attachment of unique DNA oligonucleotides.
source: Myosin V and VI were engineered with SNAP tags (Hariadi et al., 2014) for covalent attachment of unique DNA oligonucleotides.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with citation.

claim: A linear force-speed relationship is assumed for both motors in the model.
source: A linear force-speed relationship is assumed for both motors.
evidence: This is an assumption stated in the Materials and methods for the simulation.

claim: The load-dependent speed is given by v = v0 (1 − T/Fstall), where νo is the zero-strained speed, Fstall is the stall force of the stepping motor and T is the inter-motor tension.
source: The load-dependent speed is given by v = v0 (1 − T/Fstall), where νo is the zero-strained speed, Fstall is the stall force of the stepping motor (Fhigh or Flow) and T is the inter-motor tension (0 ≤ T ≤ Fstall).
evidence: This is a mathematical relationship used in the computational model.
